high doses of biosynthetically produced human C-peptide did not alter the serum concentrations of glucose, insulin and proinsulin, or the plasma concentrations of glucagon or pancreatic polypeptide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of high-dosage biosynthetic human proinsulin C-peptide on glucose tolerance in normal subjects.
the role of the C-peptide moiety in the insulin molecule in the control of pancreatic islet function.
the role of C-peptide as a regulator of insulin secretion.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
C-peptide is not an insulin secretagogue.
C-peptide has no effect on pancreatic hormone release, but that it may have a very minor inhibitory effect on insulin secretion in the early phase of an oral glucose load.
the effect of C-peptide on insulin secretion is minimal, if it occurs at all.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
C-peptide does not have a major role in insulin secretion, but may have a minor role in early insulin secretion after oral glucose ingestion.
high doses of biosynthesis human C-peptide do have a slight effect on the glucose and insulin response to an oral glucose load.
C-peptide does not affect basal insulin and glucagon secretion and does not affect overall insulin secretory response to oral and intravenous glucose.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the lack of effect of C-peptide on insulin secretion is consistent with a model where C-peptide is an inactive by-product of insulin secretion.
the insulinotropic action of C-peptide is very small, and it is not likely that C-peptide is a major determinant of insulin secretion in normal individuals.
high-dose C-peptide does not appear to be a viable therapeutic strategy for the treatment of diabetes.
